summary: This project started with a simple but inmersive question, ¿What if natural phenomena could be explained without using your eyes? The Earth Symphony is an experience made to be heard and interpret how events like multiple lightnings and a forest fire can make musical coordinated sounds without really trying to, the project was made taking into account people that don't have vision to make it feel as similar as possible to experiencing a natural phenomenon using only sounds to show how nature makes art if you pay attention, this helps people that are blind to appreciate nature in more ways.
details:
What it does

The Earth Symphony turns NASA’s scientific visualizations into music, so anyone can hear how our planet changes, even without seeing the screen. It currently has two tracks:

  • Storms of the planet, from Lightning Events Detected from the ISS 2017–2023. Each region of the world has its own voice: the Americas sound low on the left, Europe and Africa in the center, Asia and Oceania high on the right. Large lightning groups play the melody, very large ones rumble as thunder, and a background chord follows the seasons. Over land you hear an electric piano; over the ocean, a vibraphone.
  • Dixie Fire, 2021, from Spread of the Dixie Fire 2021. Active fire (red) becomes crackling, heard on the side of the screen where it burns. The fire front (yellow) becomes a melody that rises as it advances. The burned area becomes a deep bass whose volume follows the real km² curve shown in NASA’s own chart, so you can feel the scar grow, especially during the August run through Greenville.

How it works

  1. The app plays the NASA video and reads every frame live in the browser.
  2. A computer-vision algorithm sorts pixels by color, the same colors NASA uses in the visualization, and measures how much of each there is and where it is on screen.
  3. A music engine turns those measurements into sound: amount → volume and density, position → left/right panning, growth → rhythm and harmony. The harmony tightens when the fire intensifies and relaxes when it eases.

Accessibility and benefits

The whole experience is hands-free and designed for people who are blind or have low vision. You can control everything by voice (“play”, “take me to the fire”, “describe this moment”, “turn off the thunder”), and the app answers out loud. Users can choose between OpenAI’s Whisper and Chrome’s built-in speech recognition. The app also works with screen readers (ARIA labels, live announcements) and keyboard shortcuts. Every sound layer can be turned on or off, and playback can be slowed down.

Intended impact

Today, Earth science data mostly exists for people who can see it. We want to make NASA data accessible through sound, as a tool for accessibility programs, classrooms, and anyone curious about climate and natural disasters. The same approach can extend to other NASA datasets such as hurricanes, sea ice, or CO₂.

Tools and technologies

TypeScript, React, Vite, Tone.js and the Web Audio API for real-time sound, HTML Canvas for frame analysis, OpenAI Whisper (via OpenRouter, behind a serverless function so the API key stays private), the Web Speech API, and Vercel for hosting. No special hardware is needed: just a computer, a microphone and headphones.

Creativity

Instead of reading numbers aloud, we built a musical language. Sudden events sound like percussion, what advances becomes melody, and what accumulates becomes a low drone. Stereo position tells you where things happen, and harmony tells you how intense they are. We didn’t add the music on top of the data: the data is what plays it.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: we describe the limits of each dataset. For example, the ISS lightning sensor only samples each area as the station passes overhead.
  • Accuracy: the burned area uses NASA’s chart instead of on-screen pixels, so camera movement doesn’t distort it.
  • Real-world noise: a voice-activity filter ignores background noise.
  • Stability: the audio is protected so the music never distorts or stops.
  • Privacy: audio is only sent for transcription when speech is detected.
  • Use of AI: we used AI assistance (Claude) for coding, debugging, data analysis and writing. All music is generated live by our own algorithm from NASA data.
